message:
feat(update): a credential channel that refuses anyone but the process we started

NOT WIRED. Neither hop calls this yet; it is the primitive and its tests.
Saying so plainly because "written but unwired" and "written but untested in
the field" are different states and only one of them is nearly done.

Every obvious way to get a token from the signed-in application to an
elevated worker leaves it somewhere: a command line is readable by anything
that can list processes, an environment block is inherited and dumped by
crash reporters, a file has to be deleted by someone, and a log exists to be
read later. So it goes over a named pipe that lives for one attempt, and the
sender proves who it is talking to before writing anything.

The rules are one rule stated in several places -- nothing is sent until the
receiver is known to be the process we started. The pipe is created before
the child, so the name never exists unowned. FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE turns a
squatted name into a failed creation instead of a shared endpoint. One
instance, so a second connection has nowhere to land. Remote clients
rejected, because this is two processes on one machine and a remote client
is by definition neither. An explicit DACL rather than whatever the current
token happens to grant. And the client's process id compared against the
handle we hold from the launch -- held open for the whole exchange, so the
id cannot be recycled onto something else underneath the check.

Every wait has a deadline and nothing is sent after it passes: "it turned up
eventually" is not evidence of who it is. Bytes written are counted, because
one write is not a promise that all of it left, and a prefix of a credential
would arrive looking like a short one. A frame that stops in the middle is a
failure rather than a truncated token.

The tests drive the checks instead of describing them. The mismatch case
really starts another process, names it as the expected one, and connects
from this one: the refusal names both pids, the client receives nothing, and
the sender's copy comes back cleared. Next to it is the same path with the
expectation pointing at the process that does connect -- without that, the
refusal would also pass for a channel that never delivers anything to
anyone.

Found while writing it: without disconnecting on the refusal path, the
rejected client sits in a read that never completes, and whoever waits for
it hangs rather than fails. The first run stopped exactly there.
